text: Taiwan's president and legislature have separate electoral mandates. Presidential terms are four years.
notes: Constitutional text. Regular presidential cycles imply 2028 and 2032 decision points; future election outcomes are unknown.

text: Constitutional amendments and territory changes require legislative supermajorities and a referendum with affirmative votes from more than half of eligible electors.
notes: This is not a rule that every trade restriction requires a referendum.

text: Article 5-3 sets two legislative supermajority reviews and a national referendum for covered cross-Strait political agreements.
notes: Official English version. Coverage depends on constitutional or major political impact. A policy dispute may concern whether an agreement falls within this category.

text: Lai Ching-te and Hsiao Bi-khim won the 2024 presidential election with 40.05% of votes.
notes: Official indexed result; body table was not available on open.

text: The October 10, 2026 official address identifies Lai as president, Hsiao as vice president, Cho Jung-tai as premier, and Han Kuo-yu as legislature president.
notes: Dated officeholder evidence; do not carry these names unchanged into 2035.

text: A KMT statement describes its cross-Strait position as support for the ROC constitutional framework, opposition to Taiwan independence, and engagement based on the 1992 Consensus.
notes: Party self-description available in search excerpt. Competing actors dispute the meaning of the 1992 Consensus.

text: In June 2026, Cheng Li-wun said her party supported Taiwan's defense and dialogue with Beijing.
notes: Reported public position. This does not establish a policy to deny chips to the United States.

text: The TPP's leadership page lists Huang Kuo-chang as chair.
notes: Undated live page. Recheck leadership before release.

text: An election win is insufficient evidence that the winning party will cut US access to TSMC.
notes: Separate electoral victory, policy preference, legal authority, implementation and foreign response.

text: TSMC reports that its first Arizona fab began 4 nm volume production in the fourth quarter of 2024.
notes: Company report; output does not imply complete domestic US supply-chain independence.

text: TSMC reports that JASM began first-fab volume production at the end of 2024. Its 2025 report includes 3 nm in the planned Kumamoto technology range.
notes: The 3 nm entry is a plan, not evidence of current output. The 2025 annual report was released in 2026. The as-of date is the review cutoff, not the plan announcement date.

text: TSMC's board appoints and can dismiss company officers. Shareholders elect directors.
notes: Corporate governance is separate from control of Taiwan's cabinet.

text: TSMC's executive page lists C.C. Wei as chairman and CEO and Sylvia Fang as general counsel and corporate governance officer.
notes: Live page; role continuity must be checked for later dates.

text: TSMC announced a US investment plan totaling $165 billion in March 2025.
notes: Historical plan, not completed spending or the latest total.

text: On July 16, 2026, C.C. Wei announced an additional $100 billion US investment plan and declined to give a firm schedule.
notes: The schedule depends on demand and market conditions. A pledge is not operational capacity.

text: The original JASM expansion agreement assigned TSMC about 86.5% ownership, with Sony, Denso and Toyota as minority investors.
notes: Announced ownership arrangement; use as a dated corporate relationship.

text: The ESMC plan specified TSMC ownership of 70%, with Bosch, Infineon and NXP at 10% each. Planned nodes were 28/22 nm and 16/12 nm.
notes: This plan does not describe a leading-edge AI accelerator replacement fab.

text: NVIDIA's fiscal 2026 filing lists TSMC and Samsung as foundries, SK hynix, Micron and Samsung as memory suppliers, and CoWoS packaging use.
notes: A listed supplier does not imply equal shares or easy substitution for each product.

text: AMD's fiscal 2024 filing says it relied on TSMC for all microprocessor and GPU wafers at nodes of 7 nm or smaller.
notes: Historical dependence; do not assume identical 2026 shares.

text: Corporate leadership pages identify Lisa Su as AMD chair and CEO, Jensen Huang as NVIDIA founder and CEO, and Christophe Fouquet as ASML president and CEO.
notes: Live-page verification, not a promise that roles last through 2035.

text: ASML supplies EUV and DUV lithography systems and metrology and inspection systems.
notes: The report highlights establish product scope, not universal dependence on one specific tool.

text: Tokyo Electron supplies deposition, coater/developer, etch, cleaning, testing and bonding equipment.
notes: Company product description.

text: Applied Materials supplies fabrication and packaging equipment, plus field service, spare parts and factory software.
notes: Installed equipment still has service dependencies.

text: SK hynix and TSMC announced cooperation on HBM4 base dies and integration with CoWoS.
notes: An MOU and development plan; no claim of a 2026 market share.

text: Samsung reported first-generation 2 nm mass production and 4 nm HBM base-die shipments in the fourth quarter of 2025.
notes: Company report. This does not establish spare capacity for a specific displaced TSMC design.

text: The December 2024 BIS package added controls on semiconductor tools, software and high-bandwidth memory.
notes: Historical rule episode. Later amendments matter.

text: In January 2026, BIS announced case-by-case license review for H200, MI325X and similar exports to China under security conditions.
notes: Policy allows review; it does not guarantee a specific license or shipment.

text: The Netherlands announced a wider authorization requirement for some semiconductor equipment from April 1, 2025.
notes: Licensing is distinct from a blanket export ban.

text: In March 2023, METI announced a plan to add 23 semiconductor equipment items to export controls covering all regions.
notes: Search excerpt only. Historical announcement, not current law.

text: CSET divides semiconductor production into design, fabrication, and assembly, testing and packaging, with separate equipment, material, software and IP inputs.
notes: Structural taxonomy remains useful; historical market shares require updates.

text: The 2024 SIA/BCG study projected US fab capacity growth of 203% from 2022 to 2032, and a global share of 14% by 2032.
notes: All-fab capacity forecast. It is not the US share of leading-edge AI accelerators. Industry-sponsored; summary reviewed.

text: CSIS distinguishes a law-enforcement-led quarantine from a military-led blockade.
notes: Study terminology; the label does not settle international law or how others perceive the action.

text: CSIS argues that commercial compliance can give a quarantine coercive effect without stopping all trade.
notes: Scenario mechanism. The degree of private compliance is unknown.

text: CSIS describes a blockade as a difficult undertaking that could produce war with Taiwan, the United States and other states.
notes: High-level warning, not evidence of an imminent plan.

text: In the CSIS expert survey, more than 80% expected Beijing to seek better ties if it viewed Taiwan's election result favorably.
notes: Share of selected expert responses to a condition. It is not an 80% event probability.

text: The same survey found substantial US-Taiwan expert disagreement about escalation and outside intervention.
notes: Do not collapse the two respondent groups into a single calibrated estimate.

text: The publisher summary of Lights Out says its blockade games found hardship and pressure toward escalation, not a low-risk option for Beijing.
notes: Only publisher abstract in search result was reviewed. Full assumptions are an open task.

text: Rhodium's 2022 blockade scenario put well over $2 trillion in annualized economic activity at risk before sanctions and second-order effects.
notes: Assumes a complete stop to Taiwan's trade. This is not estimated GDP loss.

text: Rhodium and the Atlantic Council argue that large China sanctions would impose high global costs and require difficult coordination.
notes: Summary of conditional scenarios, not a commitment by G7 states.

text: Rhodium and the Atlantic Council argue that China has incentives for selective retaliation and for dividing a sanctions coalition.
notes: Report-level assessment. China also incurs costs; effects depend on crisis timing.

text: The CFR task force judged that chip dependence raises conflict costs but does not guarantee Taiwan's protection.
notes: A competing assessment to a strong silicon-shield claim. No causal effect size is supplied.

text: In a 2022 interview excerpt, then-chairman Mark Liu warned that force would make TSMC factories inoperable because they rely on outside connections.
notes: Executive warning. Not evidence of a kill switch or a validated universal shutdown mechanism.

text: CSIS argues that export controls can also accelerate Chinese efforts to replace or bypass US technology.
notes: Competing mechanism; summary reviewed, no quantitative offset to security benefits established.

text: Article 8 of the PRC Anti-Secession Law provides for non-peaceful means under stated conditions, including exhaustion of peaceful possibilities.
notes: Description of PRC domestic law, not endorsement of its sovereignty claims or legal authorization internationally.

text: The PRC's 2022 white-paper summary favors peaceful unification but retains the option of force.
notes: Official stated policy. It does not specify a reliable invasion date.

text: NCCU's trend series combines survey results over time and separates several preferences about Taiwan's future.
notes: Methodology inspected. Chart numbers not extracted. Party vote, identity and constitutional preference are different variables.

text: SIA's October 2026 policy blog says US fabs still need imported specialist equipment, materials, chemicals and components.
notes: Trade-association argument; useful counterevidence to claims of complete US semiconductor independence.

text: ASML's indexed fiscal 2025 filing identifies Carl Zeiss SMT as its sole supplier of certain critical optical components.
notes: Search excerpt. Direct filing fetch failed; exact categories need full-text validation before detailed modeling.

text: Capturing buildings does not ensure control of a working, internationally supported semiconductor business.
notes: Physical possession, engineers, designs, service, materials, utilities and lawful sales are distinct state variables.

text: Losing new chip deliveries is different from losing the installed US AI compute fleet.
notes: Stock-flow distinction. Replacement parts, power, software and maintenance can affect the installed fleet separately.

text: More overseas production can reduce disruption costs but its effect on Taiwan deterrence can run in either direction.
notes: Possible resilience benefit and possible loss of economic stakes. No net effect estimated.

text: A rogue-model incident could cause a Taiwan chip crisis only through further attribution and policy decisions.
notes: Original scenario hook. No reviewed source establishes that such an incident occurred or assigns its probability.

text: A government order to restrict selected exports could face fewer legal steps than a formal change of sovereignty.
notes: The corpus does not resolve the exact statutory authority for a future selective chip restriction. That is a required legal update.

text: A Taiwan disruption could reduce China's chip access as well as US access.
notes: A denial shock is not automatically a relative Chinese AI advantage.

text: A semiconductor shortage can raise pressure for negotiation, rationing and substitution as well as military escalation.
notes: Do not make war the automatic response to a supply shock.
